name: Defence & Trade
whatThisGrades: Federal action on defence spending and trade diversification away from U.S. reliance.
status: NATO 2.01% met. Trade diversification measurable: US share fell from 75.9% to 71.7%.
judgmentCall: High grade rests on defence delivery; trade gains are discounted because some improvement is market-driven.
judgmentDetail: The A- is not a blanket endorsement of the whole file. Defence spending clears the published NATO 2% threshold, while trade diversification improves enough to help the grade. Judgment enters in discounting the trade-side gain because the U.S. trade shock helped produce some diversification, and in stopping short of A. The 3.5% defence pathway is now funded (Budget 2025, $81.8B over five years; up-trigger fired on a B-5yr reading, June 2026 review), but the editor held at A- on the two remaining reasons and because the trade half is mixed — diversification improved while the overall goods deficit widened to $31.3B in 2025 (largest since 2020). Split-shadow watch: this defence-strengthening / trade-balance-deteriorating divergence is recorded as cycle 1; if it persists next cycle the tripwire promotes the dimension to a split scorecard.
construct: The degree to which the federal government has met its stated defence spending commitments and diversified Canada's trade relationships away from single-market dependency.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Defence target sustained and trade diversification materially improved away from single-market dependency.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: A- rather than A reflects Canada meeting but not materially exceeding the 2% defence floor, and trade diversification that remains partly market-driven. The 3.5% target now has a funded pathway (Budget 2025: $81.8B over five years for the CAF; the up-trigger fired on a B-5yr reading in the June 2026 editor review), so that is no longer a discount reason — but the grade held at A- on the two remaining reasons and because the trade half is mixed: diversification improved while the overall goods deficit widened 4x to $31.3B in 2025.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: The trade war simultaneously creates the diversification problem and drives some of the measured improvement, so trade gains should not be treated as purely policy-caused.

thresholds.criteria: NATO spending is confirmed at or above 2.0% of GDP and the non-U.S. export share improves by roughly five points or more, with the diversification holding beyond one-month volatility.
NATO 2% is reached or a funded pathway is in place, and the non-U.S. export share improves by roughly one to five points with corridor, procurement, or agreement execution underway.
Defence spending is rising but still below target, or trade diversification is measurable but modest and not yet durable.
Defence spending is flat or below target and trade dependence on the U.S. is unchanged or worsening.
Defence spending is cut and trade dependence deepens.

scoring.scopeNote: Intentionally keeps defence delivery and trade diversification in one file because both sit in the government's national-security and economic-resilience envelope. Read the defence and trade sub-scores with the headline because the two halves move at different speeds. This file does not grade the government's broader foreign policy posture, diplomacy, or alliance strategy beyond the published defence and trade-diversification tests.
guardrails: Confirm defence spending from NATO or equivalent official tables, not from domestic political claims alone.
Use annual trade-share movement rather than single-month export volatility when judging diversification.
The defence sub-score anchors the file; trade modifies the headline and should not hide a widening divergence between the two.

If the defence and trade sub-scores move in opposite directions, or diverge by more than 1.0 GPA points (about one full letter grade), for two consecutive monthly review cycles, promote the split shadow into live separate files.

rationale: The government set a specific NATO target, funded it ($81.8B over 5 years), and delivered on timeline — NATO confirmed all allies met the 2% target for the first time in 2025 (Canada at 2.01% per NATO expenditure tables). Trade diversification produced measurable results: US export share fell 4.2 percentage points to 71.7% in 2025, the lowest since the early 1980s; non-US goods exports rose 17.2% to an all-time high (Global Affairs Canada). The A- rather than A reflects Canada meeting but not materially exceeding the 2% floor. Policy Options flags the 3.5% GDP defence target is unfunded long-term.

name: Major Projects
whatThisGrades: How well the federal machinery for approving and delivering major infrastructure is working.
status: 15-project MPO cohort across 3 tranches. 4 projects currently sit above designated status, but only 2 have documented post-designation movement. National interest designation unused.
judgmentCall: Grade rests on documented post-designation movement, not announcement count or project desirability.
judgmentDetail: This grade does not score whether each project is good policy. It scores the federal delivery machinery: the defined MPO cohort, later-dated movement after designation, and use of the national-interest power. Judgment enters in excluding same-day promoted-stage labels from the advancement count and in applying a credit-claiming penalty where the government overstates ownership of pre-existing project progress.
construct: The effectiveness of federal institutional machinery for infrastructure project delivery.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Pipeline exists with 15 projects in the MPO cohort, but fewer than 30% show documented post-designation advancement, and the signature national-interest power remains unused.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Current C includes a credit-claiming penalty. Without that documented penalty for overstating ownership of pre-existing projects, the raw assessment would sit at C+.

activeModifiers.name: Credit-claiming penalty
activeModifiers.reason: Most projects in the cohort are pre-existing private-sector initiatives (LNG Canada Phase 2, Crawford Nickel, etc.) being expedited rather than new federal projects, and documented overclaiming pulls the raw assessment down from C+ to C.

activeModifiers.name: Timing Fairness
activeModifiers.reason: Infrastructure is multi-year and the MPO is still young, but the machinery itself is already gradeable on cohort progress.

thresholds.criteria: ≥50% of the MPO cohort shows documented advancement of ≥2 stages from designated, OR at least one project completes a full MPO cycle with documented timeline acceleration versus the pre-MPO baseline.
≥30% of the MPO cohort shows documented post-designation advancement, with at least one project in approved / permitted / under construction status.
Pipeline exists with a defined cohort, but <30% of projects show documented post-designation advancement, and no project has completed a full MPO cycle. National-interest designation unused.
Pipeline exists but no documented post-designation stage advancement is visible, OR projects are being withdrawn from the MPO process, OR the framework is being bypassed.
No functioning institutional reform is in place and the federal approval environment worsens versus the inherited baseline.

scoring.scopeNote: Grades federal approval machinery and cohort progress, not whether any specific project is normatively good or bad. Stage advancement is measured against the published stageGates ladder (designated → reviewed → approved → permitted → under_construction → completed), but only later-dated movement after referral counts toward the cohort-advancement thresholds.
guardrails: Pre-existing pipeline value does not count as new federal delivery on its own.
A referred project is not the same as a completed MPO cycle or a verified timeline gain.
Use of the national-interest designation or a documented approval-time improvement is the clearest sign that the machinery is changing outcomes.
Once enough projects reach the permitted / under-construction stages, track median approval time against the MPO's two-year target as the primary acceleration metric.
Projects that appear in the cohort with a promoted stage on the same day they are referred do not count as post-designation advancement until a later recorded transition is visible.
scoring.modifierExpiry: Timing Fairness partly applies while the MPO is still inside its first full project cycle. Until then, institution-building and cohort progress count more than completions, but announcements still do not count as delivery.

rationale: The Major Projects Office is a real institutional innovation with potentially transformative powers (Building Canada Act, C-5). The official MPO project page now lists 15 referred projects, separate from transformative strategies that are not counted in the project denominator. Of those 15 projects, 4 currently sit above designated status as of May 2026. But only 2 of 15 (~13%) show documented post-designation advancement in the recorded cohort data: Contrecœur Terminal broke ground April 9, 2026, and Darlington New Nuclear carries a later-dated approval / financing milestone. North Coast Transmission Line and Mackenzie Valley Highway have promoted stage labels in tranche-announcement sources, but not a later recorded transition after cohort entry, so they are not yet counted toward the B threshold. The remaining 11 projects sit in initial designated status. The national interest designation has never been used. The $126B headline figure primarily represents pre-existing private-sector investment decisions. The Fraser Institute and Angus Reid both found the government overstated its role. Documented cohort progress therefore sits well below the 30% threshold for B, so the C grade holds. Note: the credit-claiming penalty modifier (-0.3 GPA) is reflected in the current C grade. Without the penalty, the raw assessment would be C+, reduced to C based on documented overclaiming of pre-existing projects by Fraser Institute and Angus Reid.

name: Fiscal Health
whatThisGrades: Federal fiscal trajectory — is the spending and deficit path sustainable and credible?
status: Spring Economic Update projects a $66.9B FY 2025-26 deficit and PBO says both fiscal anchors are on track. Interest-burden, capital-budgeting, and defence-cost caveats keep the file in C range.
judgmentCall: C grade rests on improved anchor credibility, with caveats for interest burden, capital classification, and omitted defence costs.
judgmentDetail: The Spring Economic Update and PBO materially improve the fiscal-path read: the deficit-to-GDP anchor is projected to decline and the operating-balance anchor is on track. Judgment still enters in how much weight to give unresolved caveats: PBO says the capital-budgeting definitions remain imprecise, interest burden keeps rising, and not all anticipated defence spending appears to be reflected.
construct: The sustainability of the federal fiscal trajectory and the credibility of the medium-term fiscal plan.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Deficit is in the 2% to 4% of GDP range and the medium-term anchors are published and currently assessed by PBO as on track, but material caveats remain on interest burden, capital classification, and defence-cost completeness.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Straight C: the Spring Economic Update and PBO anchor assessment move the file out of D, but the deficit remains above the B threshold and PBO still flags classification, interest-burden, and defence-cost risks.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: Trade-war-era defence spending is strategically justified, but it does not excuse broader discretionary fiscal expansion such as the gas tax suspension.

thresholds.criteria: Budget is balanced or in surplus, debt-to-GDP is declining, PBO confidence is above 80%, and no rating-pressure warning is active.
Deficit is below 2% of GDP, a medium-term anchor is published, PBO confidence is between 50% and 80%, and no active rating warning is live.
Deficit is 2% to 4% of GDP, an anchor is published but PBO confidence is only 25% to 50%, or at least one rating agency is flagging a material caveat.
Deficit is above 4% of GDP, PBO confidence is below 25%, the anchor is absent or repeatedly missed, and rating pressure is active.
An actual downgrade or clear fiscal-crisis dynamic emerges.

scoring.scopeNote: Grades sustainability and credibility of the fiscal path, not whether any one spending item is morally worthwhile.
guardrails: Separate debt level from debt trajectory; manageable current debt does not rescue an unsustainable path.
A strategic defence-spending case can explain part of the expansion but not the rest of the fiscal package.

rationale: The Spring Economic Update lowers the projected FY 2025-26 deficit to $66.9B from Budget 2025's $78.3B, with PBO attributing the improvement mostly to stronger revenues and lower spending. PBO's fiscal-anchor note says the government is on track to respect both anchors: the deficit-to-GDP ratio is projected to decline from 2.1% in 2025-26 to 1.4% by 2030-31, and the operating-balance anchor is projected to be met by 2028-29. That moves the file out of D. It does not move to B because the deficit remains above the <2% GDP threshold, PBO says the capital-budgeting framework still lacks precision, interest burden rises from 10.6% to 13.2% of revenues by 2030-31, and the projections do not include all anticipated defence spending. Fitch maintained AA+/stable but previously warned that persistent fiscal expansion could raise medium-term rating pressure.

name: Economic Policy Response
whatThisGrades: Federal action on Canada's productivity and competitiveness — investment, innovation, jobs, wages.
status: Structural productivity weakness is inherited. The file now tracks tax, trade, regulatory, and funding levers explicitly, but fewer than two core levers are at authorized-or-executing stage and business investment remains near-flat.
judgmentCall: Low grade reflects execution status across policy levers, with inherited productivity weakness treated as context.
judgmentDetail: The grade is about the federal response, not Canada's inherited productivity level. Judgment enters in deciding which levers count as execution-ready: announced funds and frameworks are not treated the same as Treasury Board-authorized programs, live tax or regulatory changes, or measurable internal-trade and permitting movement. June 2026 review: the Q1 2026 technical recession and the fifth straight quarterly business-investment decline are recorded in the metrics, but the D→D- question is held pending the April 2026 GDP actual (StatCan's early estimate was +0.4%, which could revise the technical recession away) — a down-move here is data-gated, not judgment-gated.
construct: The federal posture on productivity and competitiveness across funding, tax, regulatory, and trade levers.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Across the five current core levers (AI compute, critical minerals execution, interprovincial trade implementation, regulatory-review execution, and productivity-tax competitiveness), fewer than two are clearly authorized or executing, and business investment remains near-flat without a durable turn. Each lever is assessed independently as announced, authorized, or executing per the published criteria in leverOperationalization below. Business investment is cross-referenced against StatCan GDP as primary evidence, with CSLS Canadian Productivity Review and Signal49 Research as independent productivity-analysis context.
